\chapter{There}
\label{ch:mr-there}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can write the aspirated dental \mr{थ}, and answer a where-question with tithe instead of naming a city.}

Complete MR-R39-there and run one place exchange end to end: ask kuṭhe, answer tithe, then ask kā and decline with māhīt nāhī.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[tha]{\mr{थ} — the hole in the dental row}

\label{lesson:MR-W39-tha}



\begin{quote}
Chapter three gave you \textbf{\mr{त}}, \textbf{\mr{द}}, \textbf{\mr{ध}} and \textbf{\mr{न}}. Four of a row of five. This is the fifth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script}
\begin{quote}
\mr{थ}
\end{quote}

\textbf{\mr{थ}} is \emph{tha}: \textbf{\mr{त}} with the breath let out, exactly the step you already know from \textbf{\mr{क}}/\textbf{\mr{ख}} and from \textbf{\mr{ट}}/\textbf{\mr{ठ}}. The sound is a dental \emph{t} with a puff after it — never the English \emph{th} of \emph{this} or \emph{thin}.

The shape is worth a second look, because it is the one letter in the row that does not resemble its plain partner at all. \textbf{\mr{त}} has a hook; \textbf{\mr{थ}} is a loop with a stem through it. Do not expect to derive it — learn it as its own picture.

Curled \textbf{\mr{ठ}} and dental \textbf{\mr{थ}} are the pair readers confuse: \textbf{\mr{ठ}} is a bare circle, \textbf{\mr{थ}} carries a vertical stem down the right.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy}
Copy \textbf{\mr{थ}} twice with the model visible. Then write \textbf{\mr{ठ}} beside it and check that only one of the two has a stem.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which of the two is a bare circle? (\textbf{\mr{ठ}}.) The word for \textbf{there} needs the other one, and arrives in the next lesson. End the line with \textbf{?} or \textbf{!} as before, and never both.

Source: \href{https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Deva-\%E0\%A4\%A5-order.gif}{Devanagari tha stroke order}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[tithe]{\mr{तिथे} (tithe) — there}

\label{lesson:MR-C39-tithe}



\begin{quote}
One lesson ago you learned a letter and were told the word it was for. Here it is.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \mr{तिथे}}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{तिथे}} — \emph{tithe} — \textbf{there}
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{\mr{मीरा} \mr{तिथे} \mr{आहे}.} — \emph{Mīrā tithe āhe.} — \textbf{Mira is there.}
\end{quote}

This is the first complete answer you can give to \textbf{\mr{कुठे}} without naming a city. Point across the room and say it.

Look at how it is built. \textbf{\mr{जेव्हा} … \mr{तेव्हा} …} taught you that Marathi keeps two matching stems: \textbf{\mr{ज}-} for the one you ask about and \textbf{\mr{त}-} for the one you point at. \textbf{\mr{तिथे}} is that same \textbf{\mr{त}-}, the far-pointing stem, with a place ending. It comes down from Sanskrit \textbf{\mr{तत्र}} (\emph{tatra}, \textquotedblleft{}there\textquotedblright{}).

So the shape of the language is now visible in three columns: \textbf{\mr{क}-} asks, \textbf{\mr{त}-} points away. One column is still missing, and it is the near one.

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tithe} — there
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{Mīrā tithe āhe}
  \item \emph{Recall:} greet Mira the way your named-reader message opens
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which stem points away from you? (\textbf{\mr{त}-}.) Which letter in \textbf{\mr{तिथे}} did you not have two lessons ago? (\textbf{\mr{थ}}.)

Sources: \href{https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/\%E0\%A4\%A4\%E0\%A4\%BF\%E0\%A4\%A5\%E0\%A5\%87}{Wiktionary: \mr{तिथे}}.
\end{tcolorbox}

\label{lesson:MR-R39-there}



\begin{quote}
A question and its answer landed one lesson apart. Say the pair.
\end{quote}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the line of your named-reader message that gives your own name
